newsitem.title: USA: White House condemns bombs at N. Ireland base.
newsitem.headline: White House condemns bombs at N. Ireland base.

text.p: The White House on Monday said a bomb attack on Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters was "an outrageous act" and condemned violence in the area President Bill Clinton has made a focus of peace efforts.
Irish President Mary Robinson, visiting Boston, said she extended her heartfelt sympathy to bomb victims and urged all parties to return to "the circumstances of peace."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, travelling with Clinton in Connecticut, spoke briefly to reporters about the attack south of Belfast in which two bombs exploded. He called it "an outrageous act of violence" and said the United States "joins all in the international community in condemning it."
Robinson spoke to reporters after addressing the United Nations Association of Greater Boston.

"I don't know the circumstance or the details at this time. Obviously, my sympathy, heartfelt support goes to those who have been injured, their families and their communities. I am of the view that whatever the circumstances, we have to resume the circumstances of peace," she said.

Up to 20 people were hurt in the attack. There was no immediate claim of responsibility but there was speculation in the security forces that the explosions were caused by mortars, a favoured weapon of Irish Republican guerrilla groups fighting British rule in Northern Ireland.
Spokesmen for the majority Protestant community, which wants the province to stay British, accused Irish Republican guerrilla groups of responsibility.

Clinton, who travelled to Northern Ireland last year, has made the search for peace in the region a foreign policy priority, and his intervention helped lead to cease-fires among rival guerrilla groups there in 1994.

But the Irish Republican Army (IRA) went back to war against British rule with attacks on British mainland targets in February. It has avoided targets in Northern Ireland for fear of provoking a backlash by Protestant "Loyalist" guerrillas fighting to maintain British rule of the province, security sources believe.
